entries.meaning: An alphabetical list of topics; also a number measuring something over time.
examples: Look it up in the index.
Both indexes run to forty pages.
The book has no index, which is unforgivable.
The consumer price index rose again.
All the major indices closed lower.
Several economic indices point to a slowdown.
The indices run from one to n.
She tapped the map with her index finger.

senses.head: An alphabetical list in a book
examples: Look it up in the index.
Both indexes run to forty pages.
The book has no index, which is unforgivable.

senses.head: A measure or ratio
examples: The consumer price index rose again.
All the major indices closed lower.
Several economic indices point to a slowdown.

senses.head: In mathematics — a subscript or exponent
examples: The indices run from one to n.

senses.head: index finger
examples: She tapped the map with her index finger.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the indices have risen
entries.contrast: The split is real and worth keeping. The list at the back of a book has indexes; stock markets and mathematics have indices. Both are correct in either sense, but the convention is well established.

entries.meaning: A section added at the end of a document; also the small organ attached to the intestine.
examples: The data is in Appendix C.
Three appendices follow the main report.
Full transcripts appear in the appendices.
His appendix burst on a Sunday night.
The surgeon has removed hundreds of appendixes.

senses.head: A supplementary section of a document
examples: The data is in Appendix C.
Three appendices follow the main report.
Full transcripts appear in the appendices.

senses.head: The organ
examples: His appendix burst on a Sunday night.
The surgeon has removed hundreds of appendixes.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the appendices follow the bibliography
entries.variants: appendices (sections of a document) · appendixes (body parts)
entries.contrast: Documents get appendices; surgeons remove appendixes. The distinction is conventional rather than absolute, but it is consistently observed in both publishing and medicine.

entries.meaning: A rectangular array of numbers; a surrounding medium or structure in which something develops.
examples: Multiply the two matrices in that order.
The matrix has three rows and four columns.
Not all matrices can be inverted.
We built a decision matrix to compare vendors.
Both risk matrices used the same scale.
The crystals grew in a matrix of soft clay.

senses.head: In mathematics
examples: Multiply the two matrices in that order.
The matrix has three rows and four columns.
Not all matrices can be inverted.

senses.head: A grid used for organizing information
examples: We built a decision matrix to compare vendors.
Both risk matrices used the same scale.

senses.head: A surrounding structure in which something forms
examples: The crystals grew in a matrix of soft clay.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the matrices are invertible
entries.variants: matrices in mathematics and science; matrixes occasionally in general use
entries.contrast: In mathematics matrices is effectively obligatory — ✗ matrixes will look wrong in any technical context.

entries.meaning: A point where lines or edges meet; the highest point of a shape.
examples: A triangle has three vertices.
Label each vertex with a letter.
The cube's eight vertices are equally spaced.
The model contains two million vertices.
Each vertex stores a position and a color.

senses.head: A corner point in geometry
examples: A triangle has three vertices.
Label each vertex with a letter.
The cube's eight vertices are equally spaced.

senses.head: A node in a graph or 3-D model
examples: The model contains two million vertices.
Each vertex stores a position and a color.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the vertices are connected by edges
entries.variants: vertices in mathematics and computer graphics
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with vortex, a whirling mass — the two differ by one letter and mean entirely different things.

entries.meaning: The highest point of something; the peak of a career or process.
examples: The apex of the roof is forty feet up.
Both apexes meet at the ridge line.
The trail follows the apex of the ridge.
She was at the apex of her career.
The empire reached its apex in the third century.
Clip the apex of the corner and accelerate out.

senses.head: The highest point
examples: The apex of the roof is forty feet up.
Both apexes meet at the ridge line.
The trail follows the apex of the ridge.

senses.head: The peak of a career or development
examples: She was at the apex of her career.
The empire reached its apex in the third century.

senses.head: In driving and racing
examples: Clip the apex of the corner and accelerate out.

entries.variants: apexes is standard in American English; apices is technical and rare

entries.meaning: A whirling mass of fluid or air; figuratively, something that draws things in.
examples: A vortex formed as the water drained.
Vortices trail from the wingtips.
The polar vortex pushed cold air south.
He was caught in a vortex of debt and litigation.
The scandal became a vortex that swallowed three careers.

senses.head: A whirling mass
examples: A vortex formed as the water drained.
Vortices trail from the wingtips.
The polar vortex pushed cold air south.

senses.head: Something that pulls people in
examples: He was caught in a vortex of debt and litigation.
The scandal became a vortex that swallowed three careers.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the vortices form behind the wing
entries.variants: vortices in physics and meteorology; vortexes in general use
entries.contrast: Not to be confused with vertex, a corner point. The weather term polar vortex has made this word familiar to every American who watches a winter forecast.

entries.meaning: An ancient manuscript in book form.
examples: The library holds a fourth-century codex.
Several Maya codices survived the burnings.
Each codex was copied by hand.
The codex replaced the scroll by the fourth century.
Two codices were reunited after five hundred years.

senses.head: The manuscript
examples: The library holds a fourth-century codex.
Several Maya codices survived the burnings.
Each codex was copied by hand.
The codex replaced the scroll by the fourth century.
Two codices were reunited after five hundred years.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the codices are kept in the vault
entries.contrast: A codex is a book with pages, as opposed to a scroll — the format that replaced the scroll in late antiquity.
